newsitem.title: INDIA: India's roller-coaster stocks enter "danger zone".
newsitem.headline: India's roller-coaster stocks enter "danger zone".

text.p: Indian stocks went on a roller-coaster ride on Thursday with prices soaring during an early rally then tumbling by the close on heavy profit-taking, traders said.
The benchmark 30-share index of the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) fell 193.12 points, or 5.3 percent, to end at provisional 3,453.61 after reaching 3,812.31 in morning trade.
On Thursday, trading volumes at the Bombay Stock Exchange totalled 11.77 billion rupees, slightly lower than Wednesday's record of 11.92 billion rupees.
Volumes at the rival National Stock Exchange rose to a record 23.05 billion rupees from Wednesday's 15.55 billion.
"The market is in the firm grip of the bulls...It has entered the danger zone," said Praween Napate, head of research and strategist at securities firm ING Barings.
Participants said the volatilty was due to speculation by local players who were jacking up prices of front-bench stocks.
"It's been a crazy ride, we are still recovering from it. This kind of movement is absolutely bizarre," said Neeraj Roy, head of institutional sales at Prime Broking.
"Fundamentally, nothing has changed. This was largely a money-led rally...the rise was too sharp and too steep."
Growing market optimism about positive government announcements has driven the Bombay index up more than 12 percent in the past seven sessions.
"It is very difficult to talk about market outlook at this time," Prashant Purker, head of sales at securities firm Peregrine Capital, told Reuters.
Repeated statements by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda hinting at an early announcement of a policy package for capital markets fuelled the flurry of buy orders, traders said.
"Most of the activity has been speculator-driven despite some participation by institutions," Purker said.
"The market always over-reacts...the sharp rise is due to heavy speculative buying," said Motilal Oswal, member-broker of the BSE.
"I think this is a good time for investors to churn their portfolios and sell stocks."
Brokers suggested caution after the extreme volatility, but said some investment buying might be seen after further declines in the market.
"Local liquidity is easing...which is favourable for the market," Purker said.
Napate of ING recommended a halt on buying and a phased disinvestment programme. ($1 = 35.85 rupees)
